One of the really neat things about high pressure environments is that they give us states of matter that we'd normally never encounter and which can give us insight into more conventional states. One recent example is the finding that sulfur hydride stays a superconductor at as high a temperature as 190 K when subject to very high pressure. This has lead to searches for similar compounds they may do so the same without such incredibly high pressure.

I don't think they did in the original paper, but I'd have to go back and check. There have been some followup work since then. My understanding is that experimentally finding maximum current before you go critical very difficult with these high pressure superconductors because the standard experiments are done with such tiny samples, but I'm not an expert.

Followup, original paper is here(pdf). It looks like they estimated the critical magnetic field but not the maximum current. It should be possible from the critical magnetic field to get an approximate bound on the maximum current.
